extracted.intended_audience: legislators, Congressional staff, patent attorneys, USPTO officials, inventors and industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory and normative provisions describing the America Invents Act changes to U.S. patent law, including priority rules, prior art, inventor/declarant filing mechanics, prior-user rights, and new/modified post-grant review procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-inventor-to-file priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Replaces the U.S. first-to-invent system with a new 'first-inventor-to-file' system in which, when more than one application claiming the same invention is filed, priority is based on the earlier-filed application (filing date is most relevant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The filing date (including effective filing date) becomes the objective determinative date, eliminating the need for costly interference proceedings to determine who invented first. The change is described as harmonizing with other industrialized nations and simplifying priority determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year grace period maintained
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintains a 1-year grace period for U.S. applicants: an applicant's own publication or disclosure within 1 year prior to filing will not act as prior art against their application; disclosures by others based on information obtained from the inventor within that year also will not constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee states this preserves time for applicants (especially universities and small inventors) to prepare and file applications and to encourage early disclosure. The grace period modifies how prior art is treated under the new first-inventor-to-file system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation proceeding to ensure true inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates a new administrative 'derivation' proceeding to ensure that the first person to file an application is actually a true inventor and to resolve disputes about who actually invented the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replaces interference proceedings (which determined who invented first) with a proceeding focused on whether the filer derived the invention from another (i.e., is not the true inventor). Derivation disputes are to be resolved administratively by the Patent Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art measured from filing date; 'available to the public' and removal of geographic limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art will be measured from the filing date of the application and will typically include all art that publicly exists prior to the filing date; the statute removes the 'in this country' geographic limitation for 'public use' and 'on sale' and adds the phrase 'available to the public' to clarify scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change emphasizes public accessibility as the core of prior art and aligns prior-art measurement with the filing date, rather than varied territorial limitations. The Committee explains these are consistent with converting to a first-inventor-to-file system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art exception for joint research agreements (CREATE Act intent preserved)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserves and continues the prior art exception for subject matter invented by parties to a joint research agreement, to promote joint research activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 102(c) is to be administered consistent with the intent of the Cooperative Research and Technology Enhancement Act (CREATE Act), ensuring that joint research participants are not unfairly disadvantaged by the new prior-art rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute statement in lieu of inventor's oath
rubrics_metrics.description: Amends section 115 to allow a substitute statement to be submitted in lieu of an inventor's oath when the inventor (i) is unable to submit an oath, or (ii) is unwilling to do so and is under an obligation to assign the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors in such substitute statements may later be corrected; a savings clause prevents invalidity or unenforceability challenges based solely on failure to comply with these requirements if errors are remedied. Willful false statements remain punishable under federal criminal law (18 U.S.C. §1001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee and obligated-assignee filing authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Amends section 118 to allow an assignee, an obligated assignee, or a person with a sufficient proprietary interest in the invention to file a patent application to preserve rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This update facilitates filing and prosecution of applications by corporate assignees or others with proprietary interests when inventor signatures are difficult to obtain, modernizing the statutory filing regime to reflect current assignment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded prior-user rights defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Expands the prior-user defense so it may be asserted against any patent (not just business-method patents) provided the prior user reduced the subject matter to practice and commercially used it at least 1 year before the effective filing date of the patent (or the earlier date tied to the patentee's disclosure invoking Sec. 102(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defense cannot be asserted if the subject matter was derived from the patent holder or persons in privity with the patent holder. This limited expansion is intended to balance patent-holder interests with businesses that commercially used subject matter before another party's filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination remains based on 'patents or printed publications'; Director-initiated ex parte reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexaminations continue to be available only on the basis of 'patents or printed publications.' The Act also amends ex parte reexamination to allow the Director to institute a reexamination on the Director's own initiative if a substantial new question of patentability is raised by patents or publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee intends the scope of 'patent and printed publication' prior art in amended section 301 to be coextensive with current section 102 terms. Director-initiated reexamination is an added tool for the Office to address substantial new questions of patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of patent-owner written statements in reexamination limited to claim-meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Expands the category of documents that may be cited in a reexamination proceeding to include written statements of the patent owner filed in a Federal court or USPTO proceeding, but such statements may only be considered to determine the proper meaning of the claims that are the subject of the request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee specifies these statements are not to be considered as a basis for instituting a reexamination proceeding; their use is limited to claim construction issues to prevent inconsistent claim interpretations across forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of inter partes reexamination to inter partes review (IPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Converts the previous inter partes reexamination (an examinational proceeding) into an adjudicative proceeding called 'inter partes review.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conversion is coupled with multiple procedural and substantive changes intended to make the administrative challenge process more meaningful and balanced between challengers and patent owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR institution standard: 'reasonable likelihood of success'
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevates the threshold for instituting an inter partes review from 'significant new question of patentability' to a standard requiring petitioners to present information showing that their challenge has a 'reasonable likelihood of success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfaction of this new threshold will be assessed based on information presented in both the petition and the patent owner's response, intended to reduce the high grant rate under the previous standard (which allowed ~95% of requests).

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR estoppel: 'reasonably could have raised' applied to subsequent PTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that uses inter partes review is estopped from raising in a subsequent PTO proceeding any issue that it raised or reasonably could have raised in the inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estoppel provision prevents repeated administrative challenges on issues that were or could have been addressed in the IPR, promoting finality and efficiency in PTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of the 1999 limit — all patents challengeable in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminates the prior statutory limit on challenging patents issued before 1999 in inter partes reexamination; under IPR all patents can be challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansion broadens the set of patents eligible for administrative challenge via IPR, removing a historical cutoff that had restricted relief for older patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in IPR: preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires petitioners to prove that a patent is invalid by a preponderance of the evidence in inter partes review proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the substantive burden applied to invalidity challenges in IPR and differs from some judicial standards; it is an affirmative standard the petitioner must satisfy for the PTO to rule against the patent owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing limits for instituting IPR during litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties who want to use inter partes review during litigation are required to seek a proceeding within 12 months of being served with a complaint alleging infringement, and are barred from seeking or maintaining an IPR if they file an action for a declaratory judgment that the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These timing controls limit strategic use of IPR in parallel litigation and impose a 12-month window tied to service of an infringement complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery scope in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties in inter partes review may depose witnesses submitting affidavits or declarations and seek such discovery as the Patent Office determines is otherwise necessary in the interest of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides for limited but meaningful discovery (including depositions of declarants) subject to the Office's discretion to ensure proceedings are fair and factually supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR completion deadline: 12 months (with possible 6-month extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review must be completed within 1 year of when the proceeding is instituted, except that the Office can extend this deadline by 6 months for good cause (i.e., allowing up to 18 months in total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strict timetable is intended to provide timely resolution of administrative challenges, with a narrow mechanism for extension to balance efficiency with fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to oral hearing in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party has the right to request an oral hearing as part of an inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves an adversarial element in the administrative adjudication, enabling live argument before the deciding panel when requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR adjudication by three-judge panels of APJs and direct appeal to Federal Circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes reviews will be conducted before a panel of three Administrative Patent Judges (APJs), and decisions will be appealed directly to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three-judge panel structure formalizes the adjudicative nature of IPR and provides a direct appellate path to the Federal Circuit for parties seeking review of PTO decisions.
